title: Memories of Childhood
summary: This unit brings together two autobiographical extracts by women from marginalised communities: Zitkala-Sa, a Native American, and Bama, a Tamil Dalit. Both recall a childhood experience of humiliation, one of racial and one of caste discrimination, and the spirit of resistance it awakened.

notes.heading: About the authors
notes.html:
Zitkala-Sa (1876–1938) was the pen name of Gertrude Simmons Bonnin, a Native American writer and reformer who criticised the system of boarding schools that tried to erase indigenous culture.

Bama (born 1958) is a Tamil Dalit writer from a Roman Catholic family. The extract is taken from her autobiography, which describes life in her community.

notes.heading: Part I: The Cutting of My Long Hair (summary)
notes.html:
• First day at school: The narrator arrives at a boarding school run by white people in a land of 'red apples'. It is bitterly cold. A loud bell, the clatter of shoes on bare floors and many voices speaking an unknown language disturb her; she feels her spirit straining for its lost freedom.
  • Loss of modesty: The girls are made to wear stiff shoes and closely clinging dresses, and her blanket has been taken from her shoulders, which makes her feel immodest.
  • Eating by formula: In the dining room a bell is tapped for each step: to draw the chair, to sit, to pray, to begin eating. She does not know the routine, sits too early and is embarrassed and close to tears.
  • The warning: Her friend Judewin, who knows a little English, has overheard that their long hair is to be cut. In the narrator's community short hair is worn by mourners and shingled hair by cowards, especially those captured by the enemy.
  • Resistance: She decides to struggle. She slips upstairs and hides under a bed in a dim room. She is found, dragged out kicking and scratching, and tied to a chair.
  • Defeat: She feels the cold blades against her neck and hears her thick braids being cut off. No one comforts her as her mother would have. She feels like one of many little animals driven by a herder.

notes.heading: Part II: We Too Are Human Beings (summary)
notes.html:
• The walk home: As a child in the third class, the narrator takes far longer than needed to walk home because she stops to watch everything: performing monkeys, a snake charmer, street plays, shops, sweet stalls, political speeches and hawkers.
  • The incident: One day she sees a landlord watching labourers at a threshing floor. An elder of her street comes carrying a small packet by its string, without touching it, and hands it to the landlord with a bow. She finds the sight funny.
  • The explanation: Her elder brother, Annan, who is at university, explains that the man was not being comic. People of upper castes believe they will be polluted if someone from her community touches their food. That is why the packet was held by the string.
  • Her reaction: She is saddened and then furious. She wonders why her people should fetch and carry for those who despise them, and thinks the elder should have refused.
  • Annan's advice: He tells her that because they are born into this community they are denied dignity, but if she studies and makes progress she can throw off these indignities. People will then come to her of their own accord. She studies hard, stands first in her class and gains many friends.

notes.heading: Themes and comparison
notes.html:
BasisZitkala-SaBama
Form of oppressionRacial and cultural: suppression of Native American identityCaste: the practice of untouchability
IncidentForced cutting of her long hairAn elder carrying food by its string for a landlord
Immediate responsePhysical resistance: hides, kicks, criesAnger and questioning
OutcomeOverpowered, but the protest later finds voice in her writingChannels anger into education and stands first

Common theme: children are sensitive to injustice. The seeds of rebellion are sown early, and both writers turn personal humiliation into a wider struggle for dignity.

notes.heading: Character sketches
notes.html:
Zitkala-Sa: proud of her culture, sensitive and courageous. Unlike Judewin, who says they must submit because the authorities are strong, she chooses to fight even when defeat is certain.

Bama: lively, curious and observant, with a strong sense of self-respect. She is quick to feel anger at injustice and determined enough to act on her brother's advice.

Annan: educated, calm and far-sighted; he guides his sister towards a constructive answer to discrimination.

notes.heading: Title and message
notes.html: The shared title links two childhood memories that shaped two writers. The message is that discrimination of any kind, whether based on race or caste, wounds human dignity, that oppression is noticed and resented even by the very young, and that education and courage are the surest means of resisting it.

questions.q: Why was Zitkala-Sa so upset about having her hair cut?
questions.answerHtml: Among her people long, heavy hair was a matter of pride. Only unskilled warriors captured by the enemy had their hair shingled, and short hair was worn by mourners. Cutting it meant losing her identity and being branded a coward.

questions.q: What did Bama find amusing, and how did her feeling change?
questions.answerHtml: She was amused to see an elder holding a food packet by its string and offering it respectfully to the landlord. When her brother explained that this was because of untouchability, her amusement turned into sadness and anger.

questions.q: How did Bama respond to her brother's advice?
questions.answerHtml: She took his words to heart and studied with all her energy. She stood first in her class, and because of this many people became her friends. Education became her answer to discrimination.

questions.q: The two accounts are set in distant cultures. What is the commonality of theme between them?
questions.answerHtml:
Zitkala-Sa writes of a Native American girl in a white-run school; Bama writes of a Dalit girl in a Tamil village. The places and periods differ, but the experience is the same: a child from a marginalised community is made to feel inferior by those in power.

In the first account the school strips the girl of her blanket, her moccasins and finally her long hair, attacking her cultural identity. In the second, the girl sees an elder of her community forced to carry food without touching it, and learns that her people are regarded as polluting. One is racial prejudice, the other caste prejudice; both deny human dignity.

Both girls refuse to accept this quietly. Zitkala-Sa hides and fights until she is overpowered. Bama burns with anger and then devotes herself to study. Both later became writers who spoke for their people. The common theme is that oppression is felt keenly even in childhood and gives rise to resistance.

questions.q: 'It may take a long time for oppression to be resisted, but the seeds of rebellion are sown early in life.' Justify with reference to both accounts.
questions.answerHtml:
Both narrators were small children when they first met injustice, and neither could change it then. Yet the incidents left a permanent mark.

Zitkala-Sa was told by her friend that resistance was useless. She still declared that she would not submit, hid under a bed and struggled when dragged out. She lost her hair, but not her sense of wrong. That memory later made her a writer and reformer who exposed the cruelty of such schools.

Bama did not at first understand what she saw. When her brother explained, she asked why her people should bow and serve those who thought them untouchable. Her anger found direction in his advice to study. Her success in school was her first victory, and her later writing carried the protest further.

In each case a childhood humiliation planted the determination to resist. The actual challenge to oppression came years later, but its roots lay in those early moments, which proves the statement.
